**Provisioning**: A full copy moves `{python} WorkspaceCost.trajectories_str` × `{python} WorkspaceCost.base_image_str` = `{python} WorkspaceCost.full_copy_str` before any agent runs, at least `{python} WorkspaceCost.full_copy_time_str` of drive time even at the sequential rate. A copy-on-write view starts as a mount, and only written data acquires private storage, `{python} WorkspaceCost.overlay_written_str` across all tasks, at least `{python} WorkspaceCost.overlay_time_str`. The copy moves `{python} WorkspaceCost.copy_vs_overlay_mult_str` as many bytes, and the ratio is simply the base size over the bytes each task writes. Copy-on-write makes provisioning cost track what the agent changes, not what it can see.

**First modification**: Each of `{python} WorkspaceCost.trajectories_str` independent workspaces initially shares an unchanged `{python} WorkspaceCost.fixture_str` binary fixture. Each task overwrites `{python} WorkspaceCost.modified_str` byte within that fixture. Compare two hypothetical implementations: the first copies the entire file's payload into private storage before modifying it; the second copies only the one `{python} WorkspaceCost.block_str` block containing the update. Assume that block was shared before the update and that no other block needs copying. Neither implementation uses a copy offload or compression in this accounting.

**Math**: File-granularity copying moves `{python} WorkspaceCost.trajectories_str` × `{python} WorkspaceCost.fixture_str` = `{python} WorkspaceCost.file_copy_str` of payload. Under the stipulated block-copy rule, the corresponding total is `{python} WorkspaceCost.trajectories_str` × `{python} WorkspaceCost.block_str` $\approx$ `{python} WorkspaceCost.block_copy_str`. Both support the same `{python} WorkspaceCost.logical_changes_str` of requested logical changes, and the file-granularity payload is about `{python} WorkspaceCost.file_vs_block_mult_str` larger.

**Systems insight**: Two ratios set the storage bill. Provisioning cost scales with the base size over the bytes each task writes (`{python} WorkspaceCost.copy_vs_overlay_mult_str` here), so copy-on-write wins whenever tasks change a small fraction of what they can see and loses its advantage as that fraction approaches one. First-write cost scales with the fixture size over the copying unit (about `{python} WorkspaceCost.file_vs_block_mult_str` here), independent of the edit's size, so large mutable fixtures belong on block-granular storage and large immutable ones stay read-only. The totals count payload only; metadata, journaling, and caching add traffic, so the drive-time figures are lower bounds.

:::

The design response follows the workload. Keep large immutable fixtures read-only when tests do not need to modify them. Place new logs and build outputs in bounded scratch storage rather than repeatedly modifying large shared files. When tasks genuinely change large datasets, evaluate block-level snapshots or supported extent-sharing mechanisms against their access pattern. Copy-on-write can avoid copying untouched data, but offers less benefit when most of the base changes.

Private storage still needs limits. Bound allocated bytes and file counts, account for retained logs and caches, and govern I/O work alongside the execution limits already established. A quota failure must reach the tool result as a resource failure, not a successful but mysteriously incomplete artifact. Per-workspace quotas also need host-level admission and capacity accounting: many individually bounded workspaces can exhaust a shared pool.

### Own the workspace lifetime {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-lease}

A **workspace lease**\index{Workspace lease!definition} binds the workspace to its task, owner, permitted operations, and lifetime. The runtime records which envelope, jobs, and access channels can use it. This permits the repair's edits and selected caches to remain available across turns without silently making them available to the next tenant. A new process can receive the same workspace under that lease; a new unrelated task requires its own authorized state.

The lease is an ownership and lifetime contract. Whether an earlier tool operation took effect, and whether a running test or open handle has stopped, are separate facts; the runtime establishes the latter by enforcing the end of access on the resources it controls, including already running work. The retry and pending-job distinctions from @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency and @sec-vol3-tool-calling-async still apply.

Before discarding private state, preserve only outputs the task permits to leave. For the repair, that may mean a patch relative to the pinned baseline, the resulting source version, and selected check records. Export from a stable view after relevant writers have stopped or from an appropriate snapshot, so the patch and reported version describe the same state. Resolve and validate eligible paths and artifact types within that view; a generated link must not turn an approved export into a read of an unrelated host file.

Do not archive the raw upper tree as though it were the deliverable. Deletion markers, renames, metadata, generated files, caches, and possible sensitive contents need interpretation and filtering. An exported patch is a proposed deliverable, not proof of acceptance; check records must retain which source and checks they describe. Any later application to a shared repository still needs its own authorization and action-time preconditions.

The remaining private state is then discarded under the reset policy developed in @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling. Crash-survival requirements for the workspace and its trajectory record belong to @sec-vol3-durable-execution.

Controlled artifact export governs one path out of the workspace; code running inside it has others. Source files and test artifacts may remain sensitive even when brokered credentials never enter the workspace. The next section therefore constrains network access independently of storage continuity.

## Egress Control {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-network}

Return to the injected README with credential brokering in place. The command cannot read the broker's credential from the guest, but it can still read source files needed for the repair. Sending those files to an unintended recipient would disclose information without escaping the workspace or stealing a key. **Egress control**\index{Egress control!definition} governs the channels through which executing code communicates outside its envelope. It must constrain the actual communication path, not depend on the code choosing to use a preferred client.

### Enforce the path outside the guest

A task that needs no external communication can run without an outbound network path. A task that must fetch dependencies or source needs a narrower arrangement. The runtime can expose a task-scoped service adapter, or permit access through a controlled network gateway. In either case, code inside the sandbox must not be able to reach the same external resources through an unchecked alternative.

For a networked guest, this means enforcing its permitted routes and protocols outside the guest's control. Direct sockets, additional interfaces, alternate address families, name-resolution services, and host services reachable through local channels all belong in the reachability review. A local host adapter that forwards arbitrary requests can bypass an otherwise effective network filter. The boundary must cover such forwarding as well as ordinary packets.

Setting `HTTP_PROXY` or `HTTPS_PROXY` configures only the clients that honor those settings; a program can ignore them and open a direct connection. Likewise, a packet filter sees destination addresses; it cannot tell whether the program obtained an address from a hostname or typed the address literally. Network enforcement constrains reachable endpoints, while a higher-level mediator interprets the requested service and operation. Testing the design therefore includes attempted bypasses, not merely a successful request through the preferred proxy. @Fig-vol3-network-egress applies the two enforcement points to four requests from the guest.

::: {#fig-vol3-network-egress fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Two Enforcement Points Outside the Guest**: The packet filter sees only addresses and ports, so it admits connections to the mediator and drops a direct socket or a lookup sent toward an outside resolver, whatever name the program had in mind. The mediator interprets the request. It resolves its own fixed destinations, admits the repository fetch, and adds the brokered credential, while a push or a request for another repository fails the operation grant at the same hostname. A mediator can inspect or change methods, paths, and bodies only if it makes the upstream request itself or terminates TLS; a proxy that merely forwards encrypted traffic cannot." fig-alt="Four columns labeled guest with no default route, packet filter that sees addresses and ports, mediator that binds name, operation, and fields, and outside the guest. Four requests leave the guest. A fetch of the approved repository passes the filter to the adapter, is admitted by the mediator, and reaches the approved repository with a credential added by the mediator. A push or request for another repository passes the filter but is marked operation denied at the mediator. A direct socket to a literal address is marked dropped at the filter, and a metadata or other host is marked not reached. An arbitrary name lookup from the guest is marked no resolver route at the filter, and an external DNS server is marked not reached."}
![](images/svg/network_egress_defense_in_depth.svg)
:::

### Separate destination, operation, and data

Permission to contact a service answers only one part of the disclosure question. A source-hosting service may offer repository reads, pushes, issue comments, and public uploads under the same hostname. Permission to fetch the task's repository covers that one operation, and even a permitted operation can carry information the task should not send. @Tbl-vol3-egress-filtering separates these decisions.

| Policy scope           | Question                                                              | What the restriction does not establish                     |
|:-----------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| Destination            | Which service and network endpoint may this task reach?               | Every operation offered by that service is permitted.       |
| Operation and resource | Which action may it perform on which repository, object, or endpoint? | Every submitted field or body is appropriate to disclose.   |
| Submitted data         | Which information may leave through the allowed operation?            | A scanner can recognize every sensitive encoding or misuse. |

: **Three scopes of egress policy**: Destination restrictions, operation grants, and disclosure decisions constrain different aspects of an outbound request. {#tbl-vol3-egress-filtering tbl-colwidths="[22,36,42]"}

The host-owned source-service adapter introduced with credential brokering is one concrete design. It binds a fetch to the task's identity, approved repository, read operation, and current grant before using the external credential. The guest receives the authorized source, not the credential itself. A request to push a branch or access another repository fails that operation contract even if the destination hostname is unchanged. The adapter must also restrict request fields that could turn a nominal fetch into an arbitrary data submission; the operation's name alone is not an enforcement mechanism.

A general-purpose proxy offers less semantic structure. If it relays encrypted traffic without inspecting its contents, it cannot enforce rules about hidden methods, paths, headers, or bodies. A design that inspects those fields or injects an authorization header needs a supported arrangement, such as a host-owned adapter making the request or a proxy that terminates and reestablishes TLS. The latter changes the trust and compatibility requirements for clients, including clients that pin certificates.

### Keep name resolution inside the policy

An approved name must lead to an approved connection. A destination check made before a separate, uncontrolled DNS lookup can approve one address while the client later reaches another. The mediator must bind its destination decision to the addresses actually used, cover enabled address families, and reject resolved targets outside the permitted scope. Redirects likewise require a new destination decision, or must be disabled when that decision cannot be enforced.

Host-local, private-network, and link-local destinations deserve explicit treatment because they may expose services unrelated to the task. Some cloud metadata services return credentials when the environment's configuration and caller access permit it. The containment question is whether the task should reach that service at all, and a rule written only for public internet traffic misses an allowed request redirected toward a host management service.

DNS is itself an outbound channel.[^fn-confinement-problem-lampson] If a guest can submit arbitrary names to a recursive resolver, information encoded in those names can reach an external authoritative server even when ordinary web requests are blocked. Resolution must therefore use a controlled path and a task-appropriate name policy. A service adapter can resolve its own fixed destinations without accepting arbitrary lookup names from the guest. Where guest lookups are needed, allowing an entire domain subtree can still leave the subdomain labels available to carry data. Query-rate limits and suspicious-name detection reduce and expose misuse; they bound the channel's rate, not what it carries.

[^fn-confinement-problem-lampson]: **The Confinement Problem**\index{Confinement problem}: @lampson1973note posed the problem of running a borrowed program so that it cannot leak its caller's data, and observed that a program can signal through channels never intended for communication, such as its use of shared resources. Name lookups are such a channel for a guest whose web requests are blocked. Confinement has to account for every externally observable effect of the code, and a rate limit narrows a channel's bandwidth without closing it.

### Recognize disclosure through a permitted channel

Suppose the repair task may submit a bounded diagnostic report to an approved internal service. The runtime correctly confines execution, contacts the approved destination, and invokes the permitted report operation. An injected instruction nevertheless causes the agent to include private source code in the report. Every containment boundary can work as specified while the report discloses information beyond the task's intended scope.

Narrow fields, payload limits, and content checks can reduce this opportunity. A secret scanner identifies the patterns it recognizes, and source code, customer information, or transformed secrets need not match them. The broader problem of adversarial influence and information flowing through otherwise permitted actions belongs to @sec-vol3-security. Here the requirement is to make each channel's reach and enforcement limits explicit.

These channels also have a lifetime. When the workspace lease ends, its identity must no longer authorize new requests, and the runtime must account for existing connections and pending brokered work. Closing a channel leaves information already delivered and effects already issued where they are, so preparing an envelope for another task takes more than discarding its files. The next section combines that reset obligation with the cost of keeping execution environments ready for use.

## Sandbox Pools and Reset {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling}

The repair trajectory needs its edited `src/pool.py` and test artifacts across turns. The next tenant needs neither those files nor any process, socket, or permission left by that trajectory. Pooling must preserve this distinction while reducing the wait for a new environment. A ready reserve absorbs arrivals, and an environment whose lease has ended rejoins it only after reset, whatever its last tool returned.

Two extremes bracket the design. A fresh envelope for every tool call shares no mutable state between calls but pays the full start cost on every call and must pass the workspace across each boundary explicitly. A persistent environment reused across tasks costs nothing to start, and everything accumulates in it, including whatever an injected instruction managed to plant. A pool sits between them. It keeps initialized instances in standby, leases one to a trajectory for the trajectory's whole life (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-lease), and when the lease ends treats the instance as tainted until something outside the guest has returned it to a known state or destroyed it.

### The reset contract {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-reset}

A **reset contract**\index{Reset contract!definition} states the conditions under which an execution environment may serve a new lease and the state that reset must cover, which extends well beyond the workspace directory. A command can leave a background process, an open connection, modified runtime state, or work pending in a host service. Deleting the files the agent was expected to change does not account for those objects. Ordinary operating-system features are enough to hide state from such a cleanup: a daemon that double-forked away from the task's process group, an abstract Unix socket with no file on disk, a token in the kernel keyring, a scheduled job, or a modified `git` or `pytest` earlier on the search path.

The supervisor therefore removes an ending lease from service before cleanup begins. It stops accepting new work under that lease and revokes or fences its usable authority. It must then stop or drain the owned execution, including descendants and pending host-side work covered by the boundary. A deadline or cancellation request initiates this process; confirmation that the work stopped comes from the enforcement layer. If termination or separation from a reusable resource cannot be established, that resource stays unavailable rather than returning to the pool.

Once writers are quiescent, the supervisor preserves the outputs permitted by the task's export policy. For the repair, this can include the candidate diff and bounded test artifacts tied to their source revision. An implementation that exports before execution stops needs an equivalent consistency boundary so that ongoing writes cannot silently alter what the export describes.

The supervisor next discards or restores the mutable state included in its reset contract and checks readiness before assigning a new owner. @Fig-vol3-sandbox-pool-lifecycle places this sequence in the pool's lifecycle. @Tbl-vol3-reset-architectures separates the state domains that a single “reset complete” message can otherwise obscure.

| State domain                       | Required disposition before reuse                                                                                                                     |
|:-----------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Guest execution and memory         | Stop owned work; destroy and recreate the execution instance or restore the defined memory, processor, and device state.                              |
| Workspace and storage              | Preserve eligible outputs, release old handles and mounts, and discard or restore the private state without modifying the trusted base.               |
| Network and broker authority       | Retire old sessions and lease identities; prevent delayed work from using the next tenant's resources or grants.                                      |
| Host services and attached devices | Account for queued work, buffers, and device state that guest-memory rollback does not cover; complete their separate reset or keep them unavailable. |

: **Reset spans the owned state**: An implementation must specify which objects its teardown or rollback covers and how it handles the remainder. Guest reset does not reverse effects already issued to external systems. {#tbl-vol3-reset-architectures tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

::: {#fig-vol3-sandbox-pool-lifecycle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**A Pooled Instance from Baseline to Reuse**: Instances are restored from a trusted baseline into standby, leased to one trajectory, and marked tainted when the lease ends. Reclaiming then follows the reset contract in order: fence the lease's authority, quiesce its owned work, export only permitted outputs, discard or restore the covered state, and verify that contract. Passing checks return the instance to standby, and a failed check or an incomplete teardown removes it from service. The checks test a defined contract; a clean scan for known residue does not by itself show that every mutable object was covered." fig-alt="State diagram. A trusted baseline snapshot is restored into standby, standby is leased to one trajectory, and the leased state ends in tainted, marked not ready for reuse. Tainted leads into a reclaiming container with five ordered steps: fence authority, quiesce owned work, export permitted outputs, discard or restore state, and verify reset contract. An arrow labeled contract checks pass returns from the verify step to standby, and a red arrow labeled fails leads from reclaiming to destroyed, marked removed from service."}
![](images/svg/sandbox_pool_lifecycle.svg)
:::

Destroying an execution instance and constructing a replacement from a trusted baseline avoids relying on a list of files and process names to scrub. Restoring an existing instance can also satisfy a declared reset contract, but only if restoration covers its mutable state and the separately managed resources have the required disposition. Restoring guest memory and processor registers alone says nothing about a host-side request queue or an external database update. No reset turns a previously sent request into a request that never happened; unresolved effects retain the uncertainty established in @sec-vol3-tool-calling-idempotency.

The useful asymmetry is between finding a known residue and establishing coverage. One leftover can disprove reset, while a successful scan for known leftovers cannot prove that every mutable object was handled. Readiness checks should therefore test a defined teardown or restoration contract rather than stand in for one. A failed check or incomplete teardown removes the instance from service for destruction, repair, or further investigation.

### Provisioning from a trusted baseline {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-snapshots}

A snapshot can move repeatable initialization out of the admission path. The runtime prepares a trusted environment with the required software, records the state its snapshot mechanism supports, and restores new instances from that baseline. The baseline must be compatible with the configured execution machinery and must not contain a previous tenant's private files, live credentials, or pending task work. It also needs a lifecycle: software and policy changes can make an old snapshot unsuitable even when restoration still succeeds.

Snapshot scope is an implementation property. Storage, device queues, network sessions, broker state, clocks, and randomness may require separate initialization or reset. Cloning a ready guest must not clone a usable tenant identity or assume that restored random-generator state supplies independent secrets. Before granting the next lease, the supervisor binds a fresh owner and its authorized workspace, channels, and resource limits. These steps belong in the definition of ready, not in work deferred until after untrusted code starts.

A common mechanism maps the snapshot's memory file into each new instance with private copy-on-write semantics (`mmap` with `MAP_PRIVATE`). The kernel points the new mappings at the snapshot's cached pages without copying them. Pages that no instance writes, such as guest kernel text, shared libraries, and loaded bytecode, then exist once in host memory for the whole pool, and a write fault gives the writing instance a private copy of only that page.[^fn-ksm-sidechannel-risks] This reduces duplication relative to fully private resident copies, but the shared and private portions must be measured for the actual configuration. Monitors, page tables, writable workspace memory, and restored device state still consume resources. A snapshot file's size is not itself the resident-memory cost of the pool.

[^fn-ksm-sidechannel-risks]: **Content-Dependent Memory Sharing**\index{Memory deduplication!cross-tenant timing}: Sharing a selected read-only baseline differs from dynamically merging private pages because their contents happen to match, the content-based page sharing introduced for hypervisor memory management [@waldspurger2002memory]. With cross-tenant merging, the copy-on-write delay on a write can reveal that a matching page exists in another guest, a timing channel that was shown to detect which applications and files a neighboring virtual machine had loaded [@suzaki2011memory]. A pool's memory ledger must therefore state which pages may be shared; baseline sharing is not a general guarantee against timing channels.

Lazy restoration defers loading some state until it is used.[^fn-lazy-restore-faults] That can shorten admission while moving work into the first useful command, particularly when many newly admitted instances request pages together. Compare time to usable task execution as well as time to return a lease handle. Readiness, memory sharing, and restoration latency are separate properties, each measured on its own.

[^fn-lazy-restore-faults]: **Lazy Snapshot Restore**\index{Snapshot restore!lazy paging}: A study of serverless functions restored from microVM snapshots attributed their high startup latency to page faults that bring guest memory in from disk one page at a time [@ustiugov2021benchmarking]. Recording the stable working set of pages a function touches after restore and prefetching it in one pass substantially reduced that latency. For an agent pool, the analogous working set is the interpreter, toolchain, and dependency pages the first tool call touches, and its size, not the snapshot's, sets the first command's latency.

### Pool dimensioning under bursty traffic {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-queueing}

A pool keeps a **standby reserve**\index{Standby reserve!definition}, or warm pool, of clean, unassigned instances. Admission consumes one standby and binds it to a task. Provisioning replenishes the reserve, while an ended lease remains unavailable until the reset contract is satisfied. The policy must say whether waiting tasks take precedence over rebuilding standby, how many restores may run concurrently, and what happens when execution or memory capacity is exhausted. Those choices give a reserve count its operational meaning.

Long-run occupancy and short-run readiness answer different questions. Little's law [@little1961], introduced for resident attention state in @sec-vol3-kv-workload-dynamics, applies unchanged to leases. Under stable flow with admitted arrival rate $\lambda$ and mean lease duration $T_{\text{hold}}$, the mean number of active leases is

$$
N_{\text{active}} = \lambda \, T_{\text{hold}}
$$ {#eq-vol3-pool-active}

Because a lease lasts for the whole trajectory, horizon rather than tool latency sets the size of the fleet. An environment stays held while its model deliberates and while its tests run. This is a mean, not a hard concurrency bound or a guarantee that a new arrival finds standby available. Bursts, variable durations, and delayed reclamation require an admission limit and a queueing, rejection, or deferral policy in addition to that average.

The standby reserve covers a different interval, the replenishment time $T_{\text{init}}$ needed to prepare one clean instance, and that time depends on how an instance is built. A cold start pays monitor setup, guest kernel boot, and user-space initialization in sequence, $T_{\text{cold}} = T_{\text{vmm}} + T_{\text{kernel}} + T_{\text{user}}$. For agent images the last term, which starts interpreters and loads dependencies, usually dominates. Restoring from a snapshot replaces the kernel and user-space terms with restoring saved memory mappings, processor state, and device state, so $T_{\text{init}}$ shrinks to the restore time. The substitution also changes memory traffic under a burst. $N_{\text{burst}}$ cold starts must populate $N_{\text{burst}} M_{\text{guest}}$ bytes within $T_{\text{cold}}$, while the same number of restored instances allocate only the $N_{\text{burst}} M_{\text{dirty}}$ bytes they write, spread across the time they run rather than concentrated at startup.

Suppose each admission triggers one replenishment and arrivals within a replenishment interval are approximately Poisson with mean $\lambda T_{\text{init}}$. A reserve of $N_{\text{reserve}}$ standby instances then runs dry roughly when more than $N_{\text{reserve}}$ arrivals fall within one interval. For a target probability $\epsilon$ of finding standby empty, the normal approximation to that tail gives

$$
N_{\text{reserve}} \ge \lambda T_{\text{init}} + z_{1-\epsilon}\sqrt{\lambda T_{\text{init}}}
$$ {#eq-vol3-pool-reserve}

where $z_{1-\epsilon}$ is the standard normal quantile.[^fn-square-root-staffing] The approximation holds when the mean is large; when it is small, the Poisson tail is read directly. Resident memory follows from copy-on-write sharing, with one template, private pages for each active lease, and small state for each standby:

$$
M_{\text{pool}} = M_{\text{template}} + N_{\text{active}} \, M_{\text{dirty}} + N_{\text{reserve}} \, M_{\text{standby}}
$$ {#eq-vol3-pool-memory}

Notebook \ref{nbk-08-reserve-from-arrival-rate} applies these three equations to steady arrivals.

[^fn-square-root-staffing]: **Square-Root Staffing**\index{Square-root staffing}: The reserve rule has the form of the square-root staffing rule for many-server queues, which provisions the mean load plus a margin proportional to its square root. @halfin1981heavy showed that holding the margin's coefficient fixed keeps the probability of waiting at a stable value strictly between zero and one as the offered load grows. The margin relative to the mean shrinks as $1/\sqrt{\lambda T_{\text{init}}}$, so a busy pool needs proportionally fewer spare instances than a quiet one.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-sandbox-pool-reserve
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ STEADY-ARRIVAL POOL SIZING (LITTLE'S LAW, POISSON RESERVE, COW MEMORY)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Notebook nbk-08-reserve-from-arrival-rate in
# │          @sec-vol3-sandboxes-pooling-queueing.
# │
# │ Goal: Size active leases, a standby reserve, and resident memory from an
# │       arrival rate, a lease duration, and a snapshot restore time.
# │ Show: Active leases, stockout probability for a reserve of one, and
# │       resident memory with and without copy-on-write sharing.
# │ How:  @eq-vol3-pool-active, the Poisson tail behind @eq-vol3-pool-reserve,
# │       and @eq-vol3-pool-memory.
# │
# │ Note: The registry sandbox profile values are teaching assumptions
# │       (provenance catalog), not measurements of a product.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *

def poisson_tail(mu, s):
    """P(more than s Poisson arrivals with mean mu)."""
    return 1 - sum(math.exp(-mu) * mu**k / math.factorial(k) for k in range(s + 1))

class SandboxPoolReserve:
    # 1. LOAD: illustrative coding-agent sandbox profile plus scenario inputs.
    profile = Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner
    t_init = profile.sandbox_snapshot_restore_latency  # one clean instance from snapshot
    m_guest = profile.sandbox_memory_footprint  # full private guest image
    arrival_rate = 2.0 / second  # scenario: trajectories admitted per second
    t_hold = 300 * second  # scenario: lease held for the whole trajectory
    m_dirty = 64 * MB  # scenario: private pages written per active lease
    m_standby = 8 * MB  # scenario: private state per standby instance
    reserve = 1  # standby instances evaluated
    target_miss = 1e-3  # design target for finding standby empty
    slow_factor = 10  # scenario: a cold boot an order of magnitude slower than restore

    # 2. EXECUTE: Little's law, Poisson tail for a reserve of one, memory ledger.
    n_active = (arrival_rate * t_hold).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    mu_init = (arrival_rate * t_init).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    p_dry = 1 - math.exp(-mu_init) * (1 + mu_init)  # P(two or more arrivals)
    m_private = (n_active * m_guest).to(GB)
    m_pool = (m_guest + n_active * m_dirty + reserve * m_standby).to(GB)
    cow_ratio = (m_private / m_pool).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # Sensitivity: the largest restore time a reserve of one tolerates (bisection
    # on the Poisson tail), and the reserve a slower restore would need.
    lo, hi = 0.0, 1.0
    for _ in range(60):
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if poisson_tail(mid, reserve) < target_miss else (lo, mid)
    t_init_max = (lo / arrival_rate).to("ms")
    mu_slow = mu_init * slow_factor
    reserve_slow = 1
    while poisson_tail(mu_slow, reserve_slow) >= target_miss:
        reserve_slow += 1

    # 3. GUARD: invariants the prose relies on.
    check(abs(n_active - 600) < 1e-9, "Little's law: 2/s times 300 s")
    check(p_dry < target_miss, "A reserve of one meets the stockout target")
    check(m_pool < m_private, "Copy-on-write sharing uses less memory than private images")
    check(abs(poisson_tail(mu_init, reserve) - p_dry) < 1e-12, "Tail helper matches closed form")
    check(t_init < t_init_max < 2 * t_init, "Reserve of one has less than 2x restore margin")
    check(reserve_slow == 3, "Tenfold slower restore needs a reserve of three")

    # 4. OUTPUT: formatted displays.
    t_init_str = fmt_time(t_init, unit="ms", precision=0)
    m_guest_str = fmt_memory_capacity(m_guest, unit=MiB)
    arrival_rate_str = fmt(arrival_rate.magnitude, precision=0)
    t_hold_str = fmt_time(t_hold, unit="s", precision=0)
    m_dirty_str = fmt_memory(m_dirty, unit=MB, precision=0)
    m_standby_str = fmt_memory(m_standby, unit=MB, precision=0)
    n_active_str = fmt_int(n_active)
    mu_init_str = fmt(mu_init, precision=2)
    p_dry_str = fmt_percent(p_dry, precision=3, style="prose")
    target_miss_str = fmt_percent(target_miss, precision=1, style="prose")
    m_private_str = fmt_memory(m_private, unit=GB, precision=1)
    m_pool_str = fmt_memory(m_pool, unit=GB, precision=1)
    cow_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(cow_ratio, precision=1)
    t_init_max_str = fmt_time(Q_(math.floor(t_init_max.magnitude), "ms"), unit="ms", precision=0)  # floored: conservative
    slow_factor_mult_str = fmt_multiple(slow_factor, precision=0)
    mu_slow_str = fmt(mu_slow, precision=1)
    reserve_slow_str = fmt_int(reserve_slow)
```

::: {#nbk-08-reserve-from-arrival-rate .callout-notebook title="Sizing a pool from its arrival rate"}

**Problem**: A platform admits `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.arrival_rate_str` coding trajectories per second, and each holds its lease for `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.t_hold_str`. In the chapter's illustrative sandbox profile, restoring one clean instance from its snapshot takes `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.t_init_str` and a full guest image is `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.m_guest_str`. Each active lease writes about `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.m_dirty_str` of private pages, and each standby keeps `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.m_standby_str`. Does a reserve of one keep the chance of finding standby empty below `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.target_miss_str`, and how much resident memory do the active leases need?

**Math**: By @eq-vol3-pool-active, active leases average $\lambda T_{\text{hold}}$ = `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.arrival_rate_str` per second × `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.t_hold_str` = `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.n_active_str`. Arrivals during one restore average $\lambda T_{\text{init}}$ = `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.mu_init_str`, far too small a mean for the normal approximation in @eq-vol3-pool-reserve, so the Poisson tail is read directly. A reserve of one runs dry only if two or more arrive within one restore, with probability $1 - e^{-\lambda T_{\text{init}}}(1 + \lambda T_{\text{init}}) \approx$ `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.p_dry_str`, below the target. Private guest images for every active lease would occupy about `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.m_private_str`. With copy-on-write, @eq-vol3-pool-memory gives about `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.m_pool_str`, `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.cow_ratio_mult_str` less.

**Systems insight**: Horizon, not tool latency, sets the bill. Active leases and their resident memory grow linearly in $T_{\text{hold}}$, so doubling trajectory length doubles the memory term, while copy-on-write sharing is what keeps a fleet of per-trajectory microVMs affordable. The reserve is governed instead by $\lambda T_{\text{init}}$ and is sharply sensitive to it: a reserve of one meets the target only while restore stays below about `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.t_init_max_str`, and a `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.slow_factor_mult_str` slower cold boot ($\lambda T_{\text{init}}$ = `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.mu_slow_str`) needs a reserve of `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.reserve_slow_str`. Because every attempt holds its sandbox for $T_{\text{hold}}$, sandbox residency is part of $\mathbb{E}[C_{\text{attempt}}]$ in the cost per accepted task $C_{\text{eff}}$ (@sec-vol3-intro-horizon-arithmetic), and a rejected attempt pays it again. The estimate assumes steady Poisson arrivals and prompt reclamation; the next notebook treats a burst.

:::

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_sandboxes_margin_stockout_knee.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Log-scale curve of the probability that a reserve of one standby instance runs dry, rising with restore time; a dot marks the snapshot restore below a dashed red target line, and the region past the curve's crossing of the target is shaded red."}

*A reserve of one holds only while restore stays fast; the stockout tail climbs steeply.*
:::

Notebook \ref{nbk-08-sizing-a-pre-warmed-microvm-pool} then specifies a small deterministic burst, where the steady-arrival assumptions do not hold. Its purpose is to make reserve consumption and replenishment visible when many tasks arrive together.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-sandbox-pool-sizing
#| echo: false
# What: Drain a specified burst, then restore the clean reserve.
# How: Fixed parallel restore rounds and a scoped resident-memory ledger.
import math
from mlsysim import *

class SandboxPoolSizing:
    # 1. LOAD — hypothetical policy and measured-quantity placeholders.
    burst = 12
    reserve = 4
    restore_workers = 2
    restore_time = Agents.Coding.SWE_Bench_Runner.sandbox_snapshot_restore_latency  # illustrative profile, at stated concurrency
    shared_resident = 1 * GiB
    active_private = 64 * MiB
    standby_private = 8 * MiB
    control_per_instance = 8 * MiB  # monitor, page tables, and control state
    headroom = 256 * MiB  # designated allowance, not a safety guarantee

    # 2. EXECUTE — no new arrivals, lease returns, or restore failures.
    queued = burst - reserve
    admission_rounds = math.ceil(queued / restore_workers)
    last_admission = admission_rounds * restore_time
    reserve_rounds = math.ceil(reserve / restore_workers)
    reserve_ready = last_admission + reserve_rounds * restore_time
    workers_doubled = 2 * restore_workers  # sensitivity: twice the restore concurrency
    last_admission_doubled = math.ceil(queued / workers_doubled) * restore_time
    instances = burst + reserve
    active_total = burst * active_private
    standby_total = reserve * standby_private
    control_total = instances * control_per_instance
    resident_budget = shared_resident + active_total + standby_total + control_total + headroom

    # 3. GUARD — exact scenario checks, not a stochastic availability claim.
    check(queued == 8 and admission_rounds == 4, "Reserve supplies initial admissions")
    check(last_admission == 60 * ms, "Queued work precedes reserve rebuilding")
    check(reserve_ready == 90 * ms, "Reserve replenishment takes two further rounds")
    check(last_admission_doubled == 30 * ms, "Doubling workers halves the drain")
    check(resident_budget == 2208 * MiB, "All stated residency terms are charged")

    # 4. OUTPUT — every displayed quantity has a named formatted export.
    burst_str = fmt_count(burst * count)
    reserve_str = fmt_count(reserve * count)
    workers_str = fmt_count(restore_workers * count)
    restore_str = fmt_time(restore_time, unit="ms", precision=0)
    queued_str = fmt_count(queued * count)
    rounds_str = fmt_count(admission_rounds * count)
    last_admission_str = fmt_time(last_admission, unit="ms", precision=0)
    reserve_rounds_str = fmt_count(reserve_rounds * count)
    reserve_ready_str = fmt_time(reserve_ready, unit="ms", precision=0)
    workers_doubled_str = fmt_count(workers_doubled * count)
    last_admission_doubled_str = fmt_time(last_admission_doubled, unit="ms", precision=0)
    instances_str = fmt_count(instances * count)
    shared_str = fmt_memory(shared_resident, unit=MB, precision=2)
    active_private_str = fmt_memory(active_private, unit=MB, precision=2)
    standby_private_str = fmt_memory(standby_private, unit=MB, precision=2)
    control_each_str = fmt_memory(control_per_instance, unit=MB, precision=2)
    headroom_str = fmt_memory(headroom, unit=MB, precision=2)
    active_total_str = fmt_memory(active_total, unit=MB, precision=2)
    standby_total_str = fmt_memory(standby_total, unit=MB, precision=2)
    control_total_str = fmt_memory(control_total, unit=MB, precision=2)
    resident_budget_str = fmt_memory(resident_budget, unit=MB, precision=2)
```

::: {#nbk-08-sizing-a-pre-warmed-microvm-pool .callout-notebook title="Consuming and replenishing a ready reserve"}

**Problem**: How long does a specified burst wait for clean environments, and what resident-memory allowance supports the resulting active leases and rebuilt reserve?

**Variables**: A hypothetical pool starts with `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.reserve_str` clean standby instances and no active leases. At the initial instant, `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.burst_str` tasks arrive together. The supervisor admits as many as standby permits, then prioritizes queued tasks over rebuilding the reserve. It can restore `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.workers_str` instances concurrently, each taking exactly `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.restore_str` to become ready under that concurrency. Assume sufficient execution slots for all tasks, no other arrivals, no lease returns during the calculation, and no restore failures. Handoff and dispatch time are negligible in this model; the restore interval includes the required readiness work.

**Math**: Initial admission consumes the reserve, leaving `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.burst_str` − `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.reserve_str` = `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.queued_str` tasks waiting. The workers serve those tasks in `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.rounds_str` rounds of `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.restore_str`, so the last admission occurs at `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.last_admission_str`. Rebuilding the original reserve takes another `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.reserve_rounds_str` rounds. The pool has its full reserve again at `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.reserve_ready_str`, while all `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.burst_str` admitted leases remain active. Provisioning the burst is not completing its tasks.

For an illustrative memory allowance at that final state, suppose immutable resident pages consume `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.shared_str` shared across the pool. Each active instance has `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.active_private_str` of additional private resident state, and each standby has `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.standby_private_str`. The resulting `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.instances_str` instances each require `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.control_each_str` for monitor, page-table, and control state. Reserve another `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.headroom_str` of headroom. The following ledger displays decimal MB rounded to two places; component sums and reservations use the unrounded byte quantities:

`{python} SandboxPoolSizing.shared_str` shared + `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.active_total_str` active-private + `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.standby_total_str` standby-private + `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.control_total_str` control + `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.headroom_str` headroom $\approx$ `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.resident_budget_str`.

The private-state terms include resident writable workspace pages, so the workspace is charged once. The total is a pool-residency allowance: host and broker services, storage caches, disk, and accelerator memory sit outside it, transient restore buffers must fit the stated headroom, and enforcement uses exact byte counts rather than the rounded display.

**Systems insight**: The reserve decides how many tasks start at once; restore concurrency decides how fast the rest drain. The last admission waits $\lceil (N_{\text{burst}} - N_{\text{reserve}})/w \rceil \, T_{\text{init}}$ for a burst of $N_{\text{burst}}$ tasks, a reserve of $N_{\text{reserve}}$, and $w$ restore workers, so `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.workers_doubled_str` workers instead of `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.workers_str` cut the wait from `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.last_admission_str` to `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.last_admission_doubled_str`, provided restores do not slow under the added concurrency. Each added standby admits one more task immediately and costs `{python} SandboxPoolSizing.standby_private_str` of idle private memory. The trace is deterministic; a different arrival pattern needs its own calculation.

:::

An empty reserve should therefore produce a declared wait, rejection, or deferral, not permission to hand out an unreset environment. Admission also checks capacity for active work and restoration. An instance awaiting teardown may consume memory without contributing usable standby, so reset delays belong in capacity measurements alongside restore latency and lease duration.

::: {#chk-08-pool-sizing .callout-checkpoint title="Sizing and reclaiming a pool"}

The pool equations and the reset contract answer each of these.

- [ ] **Active-lease estimate**: Arrivals double while trajectories become half as long. Estimate the change in mean active leases, and name which term of @eq-vol3-pool-memory moves.
- [ ] **Reserve sensitivity**: A cold boot replaces snapshot restore and takes an order of magnitude longer. Estimate $\lambda T_{\text{init}}$ from the inputs of Notebook \ref{nbk-08-reserve-from-arrival-rate} and decide whether a reserve of one still meets the stockout target.
- [ ] **Reset coverage**: A reclaimed instance passed a scan for leftover files, but a daemon from the previous lease still holds a socket. Which state domain of @tbl-vol3-reset-architectures failed, and may the instance return to standby?

:::

### Sandboxes as evaluation and rollout substrate {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-substrate}

The same lifecycle supports controlled evaluation and training rollouts. Benchmarks that grade a candidate patch by running the repository's own tests depend on exactly this substrate [@jimenez2024swebench]. A pinned environment and a verified reset reduce contamination from previous attempts, while protected acceptance machinery prevents candidate edits from redefining their own checks. Tests can still have writable scratch and controlled output. Whether the checks cover the task adequately is a separate question, and external services, randomness, toolchain versions, and resource conditions can also move results. @Sec-vol3-evaluation develops the acceptance and comparison methods that use this execution substrate.

Pooling makes this environment available under an explicit provisioning policy. Its contribution is bounded execution with task-local continuity and a stated reset boundary, not proof that a contained action was appropriate or that a rollout succeeded. Those distinctions also identify the misconceptions that can undermine the chapter's mechanisms when they are assembled.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-fallacies}

Containment depends on the boundary actually enforced and on the capacity provisioned to enforce it. The following mistakes confuse a useful restriction with a stronger guarantee, or a startup number with the cost of isolation.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *Removing dangerous names removes the process's authority.*

Restricted globals hide familiar entry points while reachable objects, open handles, and native code stay in the interpreter's address space (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-in-process-failure). One attribute, `total.__globals__`, recovers the supervisor's module namespace from an allowed helper, and Rice's theorem rules out a filter that is both complete and permissive. A deliberately restricted language is a different design with its own guarantees; arbitrary code in the supervisor's process shares its failure domain, and its resource consumption must be bounded outside that process.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Choosing an envelope from a platform label alone.*

A container shares a host kernel; a microVM introduces a guest kernel and a monitor boundary (@sec-vol3-sandboxes-microvms). Neither name specifies the mounts, devices, network routes, resource limits, or trusted components actually configured, and those decide reach. The Gemini CLI incident (\ref{ws-08-gemini-cli-allow-list-2025}) had an approval dialog and an allow-list and still ran in the user's own shell. Compare the configuration against the workload and threat, and read lower startup latency as a cost result rather than evidence of stronger isolation.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *The cost of strong isolation is its startup latency.*

Snapshot restore makes startup small: `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.t_init_str` in the illustrative profile. The larger cost is residency over the horizon. At `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.arrival_rate_str` trajectories per second with `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.t_hold_str` leases, `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.n_active_str` leases are active at once, and even with copy-on-write sharing they hold about `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.m_pool_str` of resident memory; private guest images would need `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.m_private_str` (Notebook \ref{nbk-08-reserve-from-arrival-rate}). Budget sandboxes by memory-seconds per trajectory, which grow with $T_{\text{hold}}$, not by boot time.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Treating an allowed destination as approval of everything sent there.*

A destination rule narrows the outbound channel; whether a request body is appropriate is a separate decision (@tbl-vol3-egress-filtering). Brokering keeps the credential out of the guest while still letting code request its use, so a permitted upload can disclose task data without stealing a key or escaping the envelope. That residual misuse is an information-flow problem for @sec-vol3-security, not a network-boundary bypass.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Fallacy**: *An empty workspace proves that a used envelope is ready for another tenant.*

Files are only one of the four state domains in @tbl-vol3-reset-architectures. A double-forked daemon, an abstract socket, a keyring token, or a shadowed `git` on the search path survives a directory cleanup, and one such leftover disproves reset while a clean scan proves nothing about coverage. The reset contract names the state the next lease could inherit, destroys or restores it, and verifies the contract before reuse; no reset reverses an external effect already issued.
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}
**Pitfall**: *Sizing the standby reserve from a restore time measured on an idle host.*

The reserve depends on $\lambda T_{\text{init}}$ through a steep Poisson tail. In the illustrative profile, a reserve of one meets a `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.target_miss_str` stockout target only while restore stays below about `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.t_init_max_str`, and a `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.slow_factor_mult_str` slower cold boot needs a reserve of `{python} SandboxPoolReserve.reserve_slow_str`. Restores that slow under concurrent load or lazy page faults move $T_{\text{init}}$ out of that range silently, so measure restore time at the concurrency the burst produces (Notebook \ref{nbk-08-sizing-a-pre-warmed-microvm-pool}).
:::

## Summary {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-summary}

The README attack exposed the gap between admitting a tool call and bounding the code it runs. A containment design must specify the resources that code may reach, the components trusted to enforce the restriction, and the limits on resource consumption. Scoped grants and credential brokers constrain access; the execution envelope enforces a boundary around running code; and the workspace preserves permitted changes across turns. Egress policy and the reset contract extend that boundary to communication and to the next lease. Startup, residency, and replenishment costs then determine how the design can be provisioned under its stated workload.

For the connection-pool repair, this means retaining the candidate edits and test artifacts without giving the task the developer's entire account or another task's mutable state. Protected checks can remain outside the editable candidate while the test process has bounded scratch space. These choices preserve the conditions under which evidence is gathered; accepting the whole repair still takes more than the targeted `r18` pass (@sec-vol3-evaluation).

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Containment includes reach and lifetime"}

* **Specify the reachable effects**: Start from the task's grant and a stated threat, then identify what executing code could read, change, disclose, or consume. Tool names and prompt instructions do not by themselves bound that reach.
* **Do not confuse restricted names with isolation**: Arbitrary code sharing the supervisor's process can reach more than its initial globals suggest. An enforced boundary must address memory and resource access as well as CPU, process, storage, and other availability limits.
* **Bind grants to enforcement**: Scope authority by operation, resource, lifetime, and budget. Attenuation narrows a derived grant without revoking a retained parent; brokering separates possession of a credential from permission to request its use.
* **Choose the envelope by what it shares**: Compare trusted components, workload compatibility, resource controls, and measured cost. Containers, user-space kernels, microVMs, and restricted bytecode make different trade-offs; device access extends the boundary that must be evaluated.
* **Preserve task work without inheriting tenant state**: A task-local workspace carries edits across turns while protecting its baseline and bounding mutable storage. Export eligible artifacts deliberately; a copy-on-write upper layer is not automatically the semantic patch to deliver.
* **Govern channels, then account for residual disclosure**: Egress enforcement must constrain bypass routes as well as the intended proxy path. Destination and operation restrictions reduce reach, but permitted requests can still carry data the task should not disclose.
* **Provision only environments ready for reuse**: Reset must stop or account for owned work, withdraw access, preserve permitted outputs, restore scoped state, and verify readiness. Active leases average arrival rate times lease duration, so horizon rather than tool latency sizes the pool, and copy-on-write sharing keeps its resident memory affordable. Pool sizing needs explicit reserve, replenishment, concurrency, and memory assumptions; mean occupancy is not a hard admission ceiling.

:::

Containment beneath the model (principle \ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}) makes the execution boundary independent of whether the model follows an instruction. It complements the typed action contract (principle \ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}): admitting a request and restricting the code that implements it are separate responsibilities. The invariant closure principle (\ref{pri-invariant-closure}) explains why every one of these bounds sits in the runtime rather than in the model's instructions. Both remain limited to the properties their enforcement actually covers, including the state and work that survive a call.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-vol3-sandboxes-history}

Running a stranger's program on a machine that holds something valuable is the oldest problem in operating-system protection. Multiprogrammed systems of the 1960s had to keep mutually suspicious programs apart on one processor, and Dennis and Van Horn answered with capabilities, unforgeable references that name an object and carry the right to use it [@dennis1966]. Lampson's access matrix separated the two ways of storing the same rights, by object or by subject [@lampson1974protection]; Anderson's reference monitor named the component that must mediate every access [@anderson1972computer]; and Saltzer and Schroeder collected the design principles, least privilege and complete mediation among them, that this chapter applies to tool code [@saltzer1975]. Lampson also saw early that confinement fails through channels nobody meant to open [@lampson1973note], and Hardy's confused deputy explained why authority derived from identity leaks through services acting on a requester's behalf [@hardy1988confused].

Each isolation envelope in this chapter descends from a line of mechanism work. @popek1974formal stated when hardware can host an efficient virtual machine monitor; the x86 architecture met that condition only after virtualization extensions added a separate guest mode [@uhlig2005intel], and KVM then turned the Linux kernel itself into a hypervisor [@kivity2007kvm]. Software fault isolation confined untrusted code inside one address space by rewriting it [@wahbe1993efficient], the idea that WebAssembly later carried into a portable format [@haas2017bringing]. System-call interposition confined unmodified helper programs [@goldberg1996secure] until its races and incomplete replication of kernel semantics were catalogued [@garfinkel2003traps], pushing enforcement back inside the kernel. Jails partitioned one kernel among tenants [@kamp2000jails], the shared-kernel lineage that later Linux containers continued, and Capsicum brought capability discipline to ordinary UNIX processes [@watson2010capsicum].

Multi-tenant cloud platforms then made isolation a cost problem. Running functions written by strangers at high density drove the search for virtual machines that start as fast as containers [@manco2017lightvm], produced reduced-device monitors built for that workload [@agache2020firecracker], and turned snapshot restore into a latency engineering discipline of its own [@ustiugov2021benchmarking]. Agent systems inherit all of this and change one assumption: the untrusted author now sits inside the loop, writing code in response to content an attacker can influence [@greshake2023not], and it holds its environment for a whole trajectory rather than a single request.

- @saltzer1975, *The Protection of Information in Computer Systems*. The source of least privilege, complete mediation, and fail-safe defaults; read it to see how little the principles have needed to change for agent runtimes.
- @lampson1973note, *A Note on the Confinement Problem*. Three pages that define confinement and classify the channels through which a confined program can still leak, the frame behind this chapter's egress and residual-disclosure arguments.
- @hardy1988confused, *The Confused Deputy*. A short case study of ambient authority failing, and the clearest argument for carrying authority in the reference a tool receives rather than in the identity it runs under.
- @popek1974formal, *Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures*. The trap-and-emulate condition that explains why a guest kernel can be contained at all, and what hardware must provide for a microVM boundary to hold.
- @garfinkel2003traps, *Traps and Pitfalls*. A catalog of how a user-level policy layer fails to confine code it merely watches, which remains the checklist for any sandbox built from system-call filters.
- @agache2020firecracker, *Firecracker*. A production microVM monitor designed for dense multi-tenant untrusted code; read it for the trade-offs among device surface, start time, and memory overhead that shape an agent sandbox pool.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From contained code to a defended agent"}

Suppose the task may publish a short diagnostic report through an approved service. Injected README text persuades the model to include private fixture contents in that report. The request uses the permitted endpoint, the broker retains its credential, and the code never escapes its envelope, yet the report discloses information the task did not authorize sharing. @Sec-vol3-security takes up this remaining problem: how untrusted information can redirect otherwise permitted operations, and how to constrain that influence and the resulting information flow.

:::
